header.competitor: Unnamed competitor (not named in the transcript)
header.incumbent: Unnamed existing payments provider whose support was a ticket form
header.tag_why: The COO decided on who picks up at minute four of an on-sale; the competitor brought named people and an on-sale on-call promise, while we offered tiered support plans she dismissed as "a queue with a faster timer."

messaging_changes.current_line: Support plans with tiered response times, up to 24/7 coverage.
messaging_changes.change: For ticketing and live-event buyers: "A name, not a queue. Your named team is on the line during your biggest moments: someone who picks up." Lead with the named people and the event-coverage commitment, not tiers or response timers. Keep the word "support" out of the headline.
messaging_changes.why: The decider dismissed our tiered plans as "a queue with a faster timer" after the competitor put named people in the room and promised on-sale on-call, and the customer's own words were "a name, not a queue" and "someone who picks up."

messaging_changes.change: New proof point for ticketing and event buyers, written for the COO or ops owner: "Your on-sale morning plan, on paper: who's watching, who you call, and what happens at minute four." Back it with a documented peak-event plan that the SE can tailor to each customer's on-sale calendar.
messaging_changes.why: The COO asked to see on paper what we do on an on-sale morning, including who's watching, who she calls and what happens at minute four, and we had nothing packaged. The trigger was payments failing four minutes in with no reply until the on-sale was over.

messaging_changes.current_line: Trusted by leading businesses; see our customer stories.
messaging_changes.change: For high-stakes-event buyers, replace logo proof with a person: "Talk to [ticketing customer] about who picked up during their biggest on-sale." This requires recruiting a ticketing or event reference who can speak to a live incident.
messaging_changes.why: The rep said "I had logos. I didn't have a person," and logos did not answer the decider's question of who handles a live on-sale.

messaging_changes.current_line: Built for developers: launch payments fast with our APIs, docs and sandbox.
messaging_changes.change: In ticketing and event deals where ops or the COO owns the decision, stop leading with developer, sandbox and uptime proof. Keep it as the CTO-track technical proof. Open the COO conversation with: "You don't buy uptime, you buy what happens when it's down."
messaging_changes.why: The sandbox load test won over Ben, the CTO, who didn't decide. Halima, who made the call in one meeting, gave it a one-word "good." and said "I don't buy uptime, I buy what happens when it's down."

trigger.insight: Failures had happened twice before and nothing changed. What triggered the switch was the CEO seeing it in public, and the incumbent's reply arriving after the on-sale was over. The evaluation was about failed response from day one, not failed throughput. Once it went executive, ownership moved from the CTO to the COO, and we kept selling to the CTO's question.
trigger.messaging: Open ticketing and event deals with the cost of an unanswered outage during a live on-sale, not with platform capability.

competitor.insight: The competitor won by putting faces in the room and promising on-sale coverage, as relayed by Ben. Whether they can actually deliver that is unverified; the rep's 'over-promised' is his own guess. After that meeting the customer's questions moved to people, and our rep kept answering with technology and tiers instead of reframing or matching. The competitor is never named, so we can't build a counter-position against them.

To the decider, M5's 'tiered response times, up to 24/7' sounded like the same ticket form that burned her, just quicker. gaps.insight: Two gaps cost us the deal. We have no packaged peak-event or on-sale runbook, and we had no reference customer who could tell her who picked up during their big event. M8's 'trusted by leading businesses' logos don't answer that. The rep says the plan was buildable with our SE and he chose not to build it, so this was partly an execution gap, not only a product gap.
gaps.messaging: Create a documented "peak event plan" (who's watching, who you call, what happens at minute four) plus a ticketing reference who can speak to a live incident, and replace logo proof with that for high-stakes-event buyers.

language.insight: The customer's vocabulary is people and moments ('a name,' 'someone who picks up,' 'on-sale morning'). Ours is products and metrics ('support plans,' 'uptime,' 'response times'). Halima's line directly rejects the uptime story the rep led with. Our word 'support' itself signals queue to this buyer.
language.messaging: Adopt the customer's framing in event-driven verticals, along the lines of "What happens when it's down: a name, not a queue," and drop "support plans" from the headline.

close.rep_takeaway: When the buyer's questions change, the deal is being re-decided. Here they moved from throughput to "who do I call at 10 on a Friday," and the person asking was the COO, not our champion. A great load test wins the CTO; it doesn't answer "who's my person." When a decider asks for something on paper, like an on-sale morning plan, build it with your SE even if it isn't a standard asset. And bring a reference person, not logos.
